items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the number of live births per 1000 people in a year”.
items.answer: Birth rate
items.markingKey: Birth rate: the number of live births per 1000 people in a year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why death rates have fallen in many LICs.
items.answer: Better health care and vaccinations, clean water and sanitation, improved food supply and nutrition, and education about hygiene.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each developed reason up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why birth rates remain high in many LICs.
items.answer: Children work on farms and support parents in old age; high infant mortality means more children are had; limited access to contraception; early marriage; religious or cultural traditions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each developed reason up to [3]

items.stem: Table 1.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. India: birth rate 17, death rate 7. Germany: birth rate 8, death rate 12. Kenya: birth rate 26, death rate 4. Name a country in the table with natural decrease and suggest why.
items.answer: Germany: very low birth rate and an ageing population with a high death rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identification; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Table 1.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. Mexico: birth rate 14, death rate 6. USA: birth rate 12, death rate 9. Brazil: birth rate 12, death rate 8. Nigeria: birth rate 36, death rate 13. (a) Identify the country with the fastest natural increase. (b) Name a country in the table with natural decrease and suggest why.
items.answer: (a) Nigeria (2.3%) (b) None of these countries has natural decrease; all have birth rates above death rates.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark identification; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: “The main reason for rapid population growth in LICs is a high birth rate.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion. You may wish to consider: death rates; DTM.
items.answer: For: High fertility (e.g. Niger about 6.7 children per woman) driven by farming needs, cultural factors and limited contraception. Against: The fall in death rates due to medicine, vaccination and clean water created the gap; a young population structure means many future parents (population momentum). Judgement: Growth comes from the gap between births and deaths; falling death rates started it but high birth rates sustain it.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: A student writes: “Natural increase is the birth rate plus the death rate.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It is the birth rate minus the death rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the make-up of a population by age group and sex”.
items.answer: Population structure
items.markingKey: Population structure: the make-up of a population by age group and sex. [1]

items.stem: Explain the problems of an ageing population for a country.
items.answer: Higher costs of pensions, health care and care homes; fewer workers paying taxes; labour shortages; higher dependency ratio; possible need for migrant workers or a later retirement age.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each developed point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the problems of a youthful population for a country.
items.answer: Need for more schools, teachers and health care for children; future need for jobs and housing; pressure on food and resources; high dependency ratio.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: For Japan or another example of a country with an ageing population, briefly describe the problems caused by an ageing population.
items.answer: Japan: About 29% of people are aged 65+ and the population has been falling since 2010; rising pension and health costs; labour shortages in care and farming; rural villages emptying; a declining number of taxpayers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Pensions, health care, workforce, dependency ratio, rural depopulation – with figures. [4]

items.stem: For Italy or another example of a country with an ageing population, briefly describe how the country is responding to its ageing population.
items.answer: Italy: Pension reforms raising the retirement age to 67; baby bonuses; reliance on migrant care workers; some villages selling houses for €1 to attract residents.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Retirement age, pensions, immigration, technology, pro-natalist measures. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of a country with an ageing population (for example Italy). Briefly describe the problems caused by an ageing population.
items.answer: Italy: About 24% aged 65+ and one of the world’s lowest fertility rates (about 1.2); high pension costs; empty villages in the south; shortages of workers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Pensions, health care, workforce, dependency ratio, rural depopulation – with figures. [4]

items.stem: Name an example of a country with an ageing population. For your chosen example, describe how the country is responding to its ageing population.
items.answer: Model answer (Italy): Pension reforms raising the retirement age to 67; baby bonuses; reliance on migrant care workers; some villages selling houses for €1 to attract residents.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Retirement age, pensions, immigration, technology, pro-natalist measures. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the make-up of a population by age group and sex”.
items.answer: Population structure
items.markingKey: Population structure: the make-up of a population by age group and sex. [1]

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 is a population pyramid for Country R. It shows that 12% of the population is aged 0-14, 69% is aged 15-64 and 19% is aged 65 and over. Calculate the dependency ratio.
Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “when there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living”.
items.answer: Overpopulation
items.markingKey: Overpopulation: when there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between overpopulation and underpopulation.
items.answer: Overpopulation: too many people for the resources and technology, leading to shortages and low living standards. Underpopulation: too few people to use resources fully, leading to labour shortages and unused resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain the effects of China’s one-child policy.
items.answer: Prevented an estimated 200-400 million births and slowed growth; but created an ageing population, a gender imbalance (more males), “4-2-1” families and labour shortages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each effect up to [3]

items.stem: For China’s one-child policy or another example of a country’s population policy, briefly describe the policy and how it was put into practice.
items.answer: China’s one-child policy: Introduced in 1979: couples were allowed one child (exceptions for rural families and minorities); rewards such as free education and better housing for one-child families; fines, loss of jobs and forced abortions or sterilisation for some who broke the rule; relaxed to two children in 2016 and three in 2021.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Aims, measures (rewards, penalties, incentives), dates. [4]

items.stem: Study your case study of a country’s population policy (for example China’s one-child policy). Briefly evaluate the success of the population policy.
items.answer: China’s one-child policy: Successful in slowing growth – fertility fell from about 2.8 to 1.7 – and helped economic growth; but it caused an ageing population, a sex ratio of about 117 boys per 100 girls at birth, human rights abuses and future labour shortages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Effects on birth/fertility rates, unintended consequences, social impacts, judgement. [4]

items.stem: Using a case study of a country’s population policy, such as China’s one-child policy, evaluate the success of the population policy.
items.answer: Model answer (China’s one-child policy): Successful in slowing growth – fertility fell from about 2.8 to 1.7 – and helped economic growth; but it caused an ageing population, a sex ratio of about 117 boys per 100 girls at birth, human rights abuses and future labour shortages.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Effects on birth/fertility rates, unintended consequences, social impacts, judgement. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: Country A has a population of 8 million. Its farmland can produce enough food for 3 million people and its water supply can support 5 million people. Based on these resources alone, is the country overpopulated?
items.answer: Overpopulated
items.markingKey: The limiting resource supports 3 million v population 8 million. [1]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the way people are spread out across an area”.
items.answer: Population distribution
items.markingKey: Population distribution: the way people are spread out across an area. [1]

items.stem: Explain why some areas are sparsely populated.
items.answer: Extreme climates (too hot, cold or dry), steep or high relief, poor soils, dense forest, lack of water, few jobs and poor access.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each factor with explanation up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why river valleys and deltas are often densely populated.
items.answer: Flat, fertile alluvial soils for farming; water for drinking and irrigation; easy transport routes; ports and trade.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 describes population density in Brazil. The south-east coast around São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro has over 100 people per km²; the north-east coast 50-100; the interior plateau 10-50; the Amazon basin in the north-west fewer than 5 people per km². Describe the distribution of population in Brazil.
items.answer: Uneven: densest on the south-east coast (over 100/km²), moderate on the north-east coast and plateau, sparse in the Amazon (under 5/km²).
items.markingKey: 1 mark pattern; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 describes population density in Brazil. The south-east coast around São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro has over 100 people per km²; the north-east coast 50-100; the interior plateau 10-50; the Amazon basin in the north-west fewer than 5 people per km². (a) Suggest physical reasons why the Amazon basin is sparsely populated. (b) Identify one disadvantage of a choropleth map for showing population density.
items.answer: (a) Dense rainforest, hot humid climate, infertile soils, flooding and disease. (b) It suggests density is the same across each whole area and changes suddenly at boundaries.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Fig. 1.3 describes population density in Brazil. The south-east coast around São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro has over 100 people per km²; the north-east coast 50-100; the interior plateau 10-50; the Amazon basin in the north-west fewer than 5 people per km². (a) Suggest human reasons why the south-east coast is densely populated. (b) Identify one disadvantage of a choropleth map for showing population density.
items.answer: (a) Jobs in industry and services in São Paulo and Rio; ports and trade; good transport; historical colonial settlement; services and universities. (b) It suggests density is the same across each whole area and changes suddenly at boundaries.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each up to [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Study Fig. 1.3, a choropleth map of Brazil. Density is highest along the south-east coast (over 100 per km²), lower in the central plateau, and lowest in the Amazon rainforest (under 5 per km²). (a) Describe the distribution of population in Brazil. (b) Suggest physical reasons why the Amazon basin is sparsely populated. (c) Identify one disadvantage of a choropleth map for showing population density.
items.answer: (a) Uneven: densest on the south-east coast (over 100/km²), moderate on the north-east coast and plateau, sparse in the Amazon (under 5/km²). (b) Dense rainforest, hot humid climate, infertile soils, flooding and disease. (c) It suggests density is the same across each whole area and changes suddenly at boundaries.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark pattern; 1 mark data [2] (b) 1 mark each up to [3] (c) [1]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the movement of people from one place to another to live, for at least a year”.
items.answer: Migration
items.markingKey: Migration: the movement of people from one place to another to live, for at least a year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why people migrate from rural areas to cities in LICs.
items.answer: Push: lack of jobs, low farm incomes, drought, few services. Pull: jobs in factories and services, higher wages, schools, health care and the perception of a better life.
items.markingKey: 1 mark push; 1 mark pull; 1 mark development [3]

items.stem: Explain the benefits of migration for the country that migrants leave.
items.answer: Remittances support families and the economy; reduced unemployment and pressure on services; returning migrants bring skills and savings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Study your case study of international migration (for example Syrian refugees, 2011 onwards). Briefly describe the impacts of the migration on the areas that people leave and the areas they move to.
items.answer: Syrian refugees, 2011 onwards: Turkey hosted about 3.5 million, Lebanon about 1.5 million (a quarter of its population), and Germany about 800 000; pressure on housing, schools and jobs; refugee camps such as Zaatari in Jordan; loss of skilled people from Syria.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. Impacts on origin and destination: economic, social, demographic, with figures. [4]

items.stem: Name one example of international migration you have studied and, for that example, describe the impacts of the migration on the areas that people leave and the areas they move to.

items.stem: For a named example of international migration that you have studied, explain the causes of the migration.
items.answer: Model answer (migration from Poland to the UK after 2004): Poland joined the EU in 2004, giving free movement; unemployment in Poland was about 19% and wages were much lower; UK had labour shortages in construction, farming and food processing.

items.stem: A student writes: “Refugees move mainly to find better-paid jobs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Refugees are forced to move by war, persecution or disaster; economic migrants move voluntarily for work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the number of deaths per 1000 people in a year”.
items.answer: Death rate
items.markingKey: Death rate: the number of deaths per 1000 people in a year. [1]

items.stem: Explain why birth rates fall as countries develop.
items.answer: More women are educated and work; contraception is available; children cost more to raise and are in education rather than working; lower infant mortality; urban lifestyles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 1.1 is a line graph of world population (billions): 1950: 2.5, 1960: 3, 1970: 3.7, 1980: 4.4, 1990: 5.3, 2000: 6.1, 2010: 6.9, 2020: 7.8. Explain why world population grew so rapidly after 1950.
items.answer: Death rates fell sharply in LICs because of vaccines, antibiotics, clean water and better food, while birth rates stayed high.
items.markingKey: 1 mark falling death rates + reason; 1 mark high birth rates [2]

items.stem: “The main reason for rapid population growth in LICs is a high birth rate.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: High fertility (e.g. Niger about 6.7 children per woman) driven by farming needs, cultural factors and limited contraception. Against: The fall in death rates due to medicine, vaccination and clean water created the gap; a young population structure means many future parents (population momentum). Judgement: Growth comes from the gap between births and deaths; falling death rates started it but high birth rates sustain it.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “a pair of horizontal bar graphs showing the percentage or number of males and females in each age group”.
items.answer: Population pyramid
items.markingKey: Population pyramid: a pair of horizontal bar graphs showing the percentage or number of males and females in each age group. [1]

items.stem: Explain why a population pyramid for an HIC has straight, vertical sides.
items.answer: Low birth and death rates mean each cohort is a similar size and most people survive to old age.
items.markingKey: 1 mark low rates; 1 mark survival [2]

items.stem: Table 1.2 shows the population structure of Country Y (% of total population). 0-14: males 9%, females 10%. 15-29: males 6%, females 5%. 30-44: males 6%, females 7%. 45-59: males 5%, females 6%. 60-74: males 10%, females 9%. 75+: males 11%, females 16%. Calculate the dependency ratio, treating 15-59 as working age.

Fig. 1.2 is a population pyramid for Country Q. It shows that 39% of the population is aged 0-14, 58% is aged 15-64 and 3% is aged 65 and over. (a) Describe the likely shape of the pyramid. (b) Explain one problem this population structure may cause.
items.answer: (a) Wide base narrowing quickly to a small top (triangular). (b) Pressure on schools and future jobs; high young dependency.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: With reference to Italy, or another example of a country with an ageing population you have studied, describe how the country is responding to its ageing population.
items.answer: Model answer (Italy): Pension reforms raising the retirement age to 67; baby bonuses; reliance on migrant care workers; some villages selling houses for €1 to attract residents.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Retirement age, pensions, immigration, technology, pro-natalist measures. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “overpopulation”?
options: When there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living.
A government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate.
The number of people that gives the highest standard of living for the resources and technology available.
When there are too few people to use the resources of an area efficiently.
items.answer: When there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living.
items.markingKey: Overpopulation: when there are too many people for the resources and technology available to maintain a good standard of living. [1]

items.stem: Explain why some countries introduce pro-natalist policies.
items.answer: Low birth rates and an ageing population lead to labour shortages and fewer taxpayers to pay for pensions; the population may decline.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark consequence [2]

items.stem: Country A has a population of 12 million. Its farmland can produce enough food for 6 million people and its water supply can support 10 million people. Suggest two ways the country could support more people without reducing the population.
items.answer: Importing food; irrigation and higher-yielding crops; desalination or water recycling; reducing waste; trade using other resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Densely populated countries are always poor.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Singapore and the Netherlands are very densely populated but wealthy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows the population and area of regions in a country. Region A: population 2 900 000, area 30 000 km². Region B: population 700 000, area 183 000 km². Region C: population 2 000 000, area 10 000 km². Suggest physical factors that might explain the low density in Region B.
items.answer: Mountains or steep slopes; desert or very cold climate; poor soils; dense forest; lack of water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [2]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows the population and area of regions in a country. Region A: population 3 400 000, area 10 000 km². Region B: population 1 500 000, area 134 000 km². Region C: population 7 400 000, area 10 000 km². Region D: population 20 000, area 226 000 km². (a) Identify the most densely and the most sparsely populated regions. (b) Calculate the overall population density of the country shown.
items.answer: (a) Densest: Region C; sparsest: Region D (b) 32.4 per km²

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Remittances can be an important source of income for LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. In some countries, e.g. Nepal and Tajikistan, they equal a quarter or more of GDP.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the problems migration can cause for the country that migrants leave.
items.answer: Loss of young, skilled workers (brain drain); ageing and unbalanced population; farms abandoned; families split.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: Country P has a population of 20 million, a birth rate of 22 per 1000 and a death rate of 7 per 1000. In one year 253 000 people immigrated and 154 000 emigrated. (a) Calculate the net migration. (b) Calculate the total population change for the year.
items.markingKey: (a) immigrants − emigrants = 253 000 − 154 000 = 99 000 [1] (b) natural increase + net migration = 300 000 + (99 000) = 399 000 [1]

items.stem: Ines argues that international migration brings more benefits than problems to host countries. How far do you agree? Give evidence for and against before reaching a judgement. You may wish to consider: refugees; ageing populations.
items.answer: For: Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes, start businesses and support ageing populations (e.g. Polish workers in the UK, migrant workers in the Gulf). Against: Rapid inflows put pressure on housing, schools and health care; tension and exploitation of migrant workers; refugee crises strain poorer host countries such as Lebanon. Judgement: Usually the economic benefits outweigh the problems in the long run, especially for HICs, but sudden refugee flows can overwhelm poorer hosts.
items.markingKey: Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, generalised statements. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements with some explanation and some reference to examples. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, well-developed answer with accurate, place-specific detail and a clear judgement. [7]

items.stem: “International migration brings more benefits than problems to host countries.” Discuss this view, using named examples, and reach a supported conclusion.
items.answer: For: Migrants fill labour shortages, pay taxes, start businesses and support ageing populations (e.g. Polish workers in the UK, migrant workers in the Gulf). Against: Rapid inflows put pressure on housing, schools and health care; tension and exploitation of migrant workers; refugee crises strain poorer host countries such as Lebanon. Judgement: Usually the economic benefits outweigh the problems in the long run, especially for HICs, but sudden refugee flows can overwhelm poorer hosts.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the difference between the birth rate and the death rate when births exceed deaths, usually given as a percentage”.
items.answer: Natural increase
items.markingKey: Natural increase: the difference between the birth rate and the death rate when births exceed deaths, usually given as a percentage. [1]

items.stem: A classmate claims: “Migration does not affect a country’s rate of natural increase.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Natural increase only compares births and deaths; total population change also includes migration.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 1.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. USA: birth rate 11, death rate 10. Egypt: birth rate 22, death rate 5. Italy: birth rate 8, death rate 12. Name a country in the table with natural decrease and suggest why.
items.answer: Italy: very low birth rate and an ageing population with a high death rate.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identification; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: Table 1.1 shows birth and death rates (per 1000 per year) for selected countries. Italy: birth rate 8, death rate 11. Germany: birth rate 9, death rate 13. Bangladesh: birth rate 18, death rate 4. India: birth rate 15, death rate 7. (a) Calculate the rate of natural increase (%) for each country. (b) Identify the country with the fastest natural increase. (c) Name a country in the table with natural decrease and suggest why. (d) Suggest which stage of the demographic transition model Bangladesh is in. Give a reason.
items.answer: (a) Italy -0.3%; Germany -0.4%; Bangladesh 1.4%; India 0.8% (b) Bangladesh (1.4%) (c) Italy: very low birth rate and an ageing population with a high death rate. (d) Stage 3 or 4: birth rate falling towards the low death rate.
items.markingKey: (a) (birth rate − death rate) ÷ 10 for each; 1 mark for two correct, 2 marks all correct [2] (b) [1] (c) 1 mark identification; 1 mark reason [2] (d) 1 mark stage; 1 mark reason using data [2]

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the number of dependants (aged 0-14 and 65+) for every 100 people of working age (15-64)”.
items.answer: Dependency ratio
items.markingKey: Dependency ratio: the number of dependants (aged 0-14 and 65+) for every 100 people of working age (15-64). [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “A high dependency ratio always means a country has many elderly people.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It may be high because of many young dependants, as in most LICs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 is a population pyramid for Country P. It shows that 16% of the population is aged 0-14, 55% is aged 15-64 and 29% is aged 65 and over. Explain one problem this population structure may cause.
items.answer: Rising pension and health-care costs with fewer taxpayers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark problem; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: Fig. 1.2 is a population pyramid for Country P. It shows that 15% of the population is aged 0-14, 63% is aged 15-64 and 22% is aged 65 and over. (a) Describe the likely shape of the pyramid. (b) Explain one problem this population structure may cause.
items.answer: (a) Narrow base, straight sides and a wide top. (b) Rising pension and health-care costs with fewer taxpayers.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark problem; 1 mark development [2]

items.stem: With reference to Italy, or another example of a country with an ageing population you have studied, describe the problems caused by an ageing population.
items.answer: Model answer (Italy): About 24% aged 65+ and one of the world’s lowest fertility rates (about 1.2); high pension costs; empty villages in the south; shortages of workers.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Pensions, health care, workforce, dependency ratio, rural depopulation – with figures. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “underpopulation”?
options: A government policy that aims to reduce the birth rate.
The number of people that gives the highest standard of living for the resources and technology available.
A government policy that aims to increase the birth rate.
When there are too few people to use the resources of an area efficiently.
items.answer: When there are too few people to use the resources of an area efficiently.
items.markingKey: Underpopulation: when there are too few people to use the resources of an area efficiently. [1]

items.stem: Describe the signs of overpopulation in an area.
items.answer: Food and water shortages, unemployment, overcrowded housing and informal settlements, pressure on schools and health care, environmental damage.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each up to [3]

items.stem: An island state has a population of 12 million. Its farmland can produce enough food for 3 million people and its water supply can support 10 million people. State whether the country is overpopulated, using the data.
items.answer: Overpopulated: resources support 3 million and the population is 12 million.
items.markingKey: 1 mark judgement; 1 mark data [2]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Population distribution is uneven in most countries.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. People cluster in cities, valleys and coastal plains and avoid deserts, mountains and dense forest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows the population and area of regions in a country. Region A: population 5 300 000, area 9 000 km². Region B: population 1 300 000, area 41 000 km². Region C: population 8 100 000, area 20 000 km². Calculate the overall population density of the country shown.
items.answer: 210 per km²

items.stem: Table 1.3 shows the population and area of regions in a country. Region A: population 5 200 000, area 24 000 km². Region B: population 900 000, area 71 000 km². Region C: population 7 600 000, area 17 000 km². Region D: population 10 000, area 283 000 km². (a) Calculate the population density of each region. (b) Calculate the overall population density of the country shown.
items.answer: (a) Region A 216.7 per km²; Region B 12.7 per km²; Region C 447.1 per km²; Region D 0.04 per km² (b) 34.7 per km²
items.markingKey: (a) population ÷ area for each; 1 mark for two correct, 2 marks all correct [2] (b) 13 710 000 ÷ 395 000 [2]

items.stem: A revision website states: “Most migrants move from HICs to LICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Most international migrants move to HICs or to richer neighbouring countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Hana is considering moving from a rural area to a city. Classify each statement as a push or a pull factor. A: Relatives already live in the city and can help. B: Schools and hospitals in the city are better. C: Wages are five times higher abroad. D: The city offers bright lights and entertainment. E: Flooding destroyed the village. F: The government is persecuting religious minorities.
items.answer: A pull; B pull; C pull; D pull; E push; F push
items.markingKey: 1 mark for every two correct [3]

items.stem: Country R has a population of 12 million, a birth rate of 17 per 1000 and a death rate of 7 per 1000. In one year 217 000 people immigrated and 123 000 emigrated. (a) Calculate the net migration. (b) Calculate the total population change for the year.
items.markingKey: (a) immigrants − emigrants = 217 000 − 123 000 = 94 000 [1] (b) natural increase + net migration = 120 000 + (94 000) = 214 000 [1]

items.stem: Name an example of international migration. For your chosen example, explain the causes of the migration.
items.answer: Model answer (Syrian refugees, 2011 onwards): Civil war from 2011, bombing of cities such as Aleppo and Homs, persecution and the collapse of services forced over 6 million people to flee abroad and millions more to move within Syria.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Push and pull factors, economic, social, political, environmental, linked to named places. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]

items.stem: For a named example of international migration that you have studied, describe the impacts of the migration on the areas that people leave and the areas they move to.
items.answer: Model answer (Syrian refugees, 2011 onwards): Turkey hosted about 3.5 million, Lebanon about 1.5 million (a quarter of its population), and Germany about 800 000; pressure on housing, schools and jobs; refugee camps such as Zaatari in Jordan; loss of skilled people from Syria.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Impacts on origin and destination: economic, social, demographic, with figures. Levels marking. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple statements, not place-specific. Level 2 (4-6 marks): developed statements, with some reference to the named example. Level 3 (7 marks): comprehensive, developed statements with accurate place-specific detail (names, figures, dates) from the named example. [7]
